content: Systemic corticosteroids are commonly used in the treatment of children with severe acute asthma who require hospitalization. However, there is no clear agreement on the specific corticosteroid agent, the appropriate dose, or the best route of administration. The primary objective of this analysis was to evaluate the effectiveness of systemic corticosteroids—whether administered orally, intravenously, or intramuscularly—compared to placebo or inhaled corticosteroids in managing acute asthma in children. To gather relevant data, controlled trials were identified through the Cochrane Airways Review Group Register, manual searches of respiratory journals, examination of reference lists, and communication with experts and pharmaceutical companies. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children aged 1 to 18 years with severe acute asthma requiring hospital admission were included. These studies assessed the use of oral, inhaled, intravenous, or intramuscular corticosteroids. Data extraction and analysis were conducted by two independent reviewers using a standardized form. All numerical data, calculations, and graphical interpretations were independently verified to ensure accuracy. Seven trials were included in the analysis, involving a total of 426 children. Of these, 274 children received oral prednisone versus placebo, 106 received intravenous corticosteroids versus placebo, and 46 were treated with nebulized budesonide versus oral prednisolone. A significant proportion of children treated with systemic corticosteroids were discharged earlier than those in the placebo group, with an odds ratio (OR) of 7.00 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.98 to 16.45) and a number needed to treat (NNT) of 3 (95% CI: 2 to 8). The duration of hospital stay was shorter in the corticosteroid-treated groups, with a weighted mean difference (WMD) of -8.75 hours (95% CI: -19.23 to 1.74). There were no significant differences observed between the groups in terms of pulmonary function or oxygen saturation levels. However, children treated with systemic corticosteroids were less likely to experience a relapse within one to three months following hospitalization, with an OR of 0.19 (95% CI: 0.07 to 0.55) and an NNT of 3 (95% CI: 2 to 7). A single small study comparing nebulized budesonide to oral prednisone did not demonstrate either equivalence or a significant difference between the two therapies. In conclusion, systemic corticosteroids appear to provide certain benefits for children hospitalized with acute asthma, including earlier discharge and a reduced likelihood of relapse. At present, inhaled or nebulized corticosteroids cannot be considered equivalent to systemic corticosteroids. Further research is needed to determine the optimal corticosteroid agent, dose, and route of administration for this patient population.
